name.text: Mixing ratio for a target price

questiontext.text:
A trader mixes {@G[1]@} at Ksh \({@ksh(p1)@}\) a kilogram with {@G[2]@} at Ksh \({@ksh(p2)@}\) a kilogram so that the mixture costs Ksh \({@ksh(p)@}\) a kilogram. Find the ratio of the masses, {@G[3]@} : {@G[4]@}, in its simplest form.

[[input:ans1]] : [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans1]] [[validation:ans2]]

[[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Balance the distances from the target price. Each kilogram of {@G[3]@} is \({@ksh(p)@} - {@ksh(p1)@} = {@dc@}\) shillings below the target; each kilogram of {@G[4]@} is \({@ksh(p2)@} - {@ksh(p)@} = {@dd2@}\) shillings above it. Cross the distances over:

\[\text{cheap} : \text{dear} = {@dd2@} : {@dc@} = {@r1c@} : {@r2c@}\]

Check: \(({@r1c@} \times {@ksh(p1)@} + {@r2c@} \times {@ksh(p2)@}) \div {@r1c+r2c@} = {@ksh(p)@}\). The target is nearer the {@nr@} grade, so more of that grade is used.

questiondescription.text:
Compound Proportions: mixing ratio for a target price

Grade 12 CBE Core 1.3 / Essential 1.2 (C d; E e): Find, in its simplest form, the ratio in which two grades must be mixed to make a given price.

Core and Essential

This question is original to this project.

truefeedback.text: Your ratio gives the right price, but it is not in its simplest form: both numbers can be divided by \({@gcd(ans1,ans2)@}\).
Your ratio is the wrong way round. The target is nearer the {@nr@} grade, so more of that grade is used.

That is the ratio of the prices. Test it: \({@ans1@}\) kg of {@G[3]@} with \({@ans2@}\) kg of {@G[4]@} would cost {@ab(mc,2)@}Ksh \({@ksh(mc)@}\) a kilogram, not Ksh \({@ksh(p)@}\). Use how far each price is from the target instead.

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(mc=0)"]]

Each part of a ratio must be a positive whole number.

[[elif test="is(mc=p)"]]

Your ratio gives the right price, but each part must be a positive whole number, with the ratio in its simplest form.

[[else]]

Test your ratio: \({@ans1@}\) kg of {@G[3]@} with \({@ans2@}\) kg of {@G[4]@} costs \({@ans1@} \times {@ksh(p1)@} + {@ans2@} \times {@ksh(p2)@}\) shillings for \({@ans1+ans2@}\) kg, which is {@ab(mc,2)@}Ksh \({@ksh(mc)@}\) a kilogram, not Ksh \({@ksh(p)@}\). Use how far each price is from the target.

[[/if]]
